catalog_quote: but in a language such as Tirāhī which has no standard, they are much more considerable, and we find the same word pronounced by these men in very different ways at different times. For instance, for 'man' the speakers at one time said ādᵃm and at another time adam; for 'good,' at one time braḍa, and at another breḍa; and for 'child,' at one time badᵃna, with no stress on the penultimate, and at another time badána, with] a strong stress on the penultimate. Under such circumstances, it would at present be dangerous to lay down any rules for a standard pronunciation of Tirāhī, and we must await further information on the subject. Suffice it to say here that this uncertainty occurs chiefly in regard to the vowels, and that the consonantal system appears to be pretty constant and to agree with that of the other Dardic languages.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only primary description declines to state a stress rule: the two (illiterate) speakers recorded by Stein stressed the same word differently on different occasions (badᵃna with no penultimate stress vs badána with strong penultimate stress), and Grierson says it would be 'dangerous to lay down any rules'. No later source (Morgenstierne 1934, Edel'man 1983, Grjunberg & Edel'man 1999) states where stress falls; Morgenstierne's vocabulary marks acute accents on many words (badána, myána, kuxió) without explaining them.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement itself is that stress placement varied between tokens of the same word and no rule can be given.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated citation forms and short sentences elicited in Peshawar (1921) by Aurel Stein from two illiterate speakers originally from Jaba (Ningrahar/Nangarhar); Grierson explicitly attributes the variation to collocation in the sentence and the speaker's mood. Print shows a stray mark after 'with' ('with] a strong stress'), transcribed here as 'with a strong stress'.
new_statements.identity_note: Tirahi (tira1253, ISO tra; alt. Dardu, Tirāhī), Dardic, villages of Jaba/Mitarani/Supai south-east of Jalalabad, Ningrahar (Nangarhar), Afghanistan; now dormant/extinct (Glottolog AES). All descriptions rest on two corpora: Stein 1921 (two illiterate speakers from Jaba, recorded in Peshawar; published by Grierson 1925/1927) and Morgenstierne 1929 (one old speaker from Jaba, published 1934). Grjunberg & Edel'man 1999 sec. 6.0: no dialect division.

sources.note: Silent on stress placement. Introduction pp. 161-170 covers morphology, loans, historical sound changes (c/z, x/gh, aspiration, v->b, clusters) and affinities; no sentence on stress or accent (a full-text search for stress/accent/cent/tress empty; pp. 161-170 read in full). Vocabulary items carry acute accents (badána, myána, kuxió, pazémā) but the marking is never explained.

No phonology section; only 'much influence from Pashto in phonology, lexicon and even morphology'. Cites Grierson 1925, Cardona & Jain 2003 pp. 857-859, Morgenstierne 1934 (Acta Orientalia 11-12), Stein 1925, Turner 1934.
